review: Europe's best-selling EV isn't winning on charm. The Juniper facelift fixed the two things owners actually complained about: a rear axle that punished every expansion joint, and cabin noise. Double glazing and softer damping make it a genuinely relaxed autobahn car, and 21.7 kWh/100 km over 800 km of mixed German driving is respectable for a 4.79 m crossover. The Standard opens the range at €39,990 with 534 km WLTP; €50,970 buys the Long Range RWD with 622 km and 250 kW peaks. That 400-volt pack tops out near 230 kW then tapers hard, so roughly 30 minutes to 80% is the reality — the real advantage is Supercharger reliability, not raw speed. Practicality stays untouchable: 854 litres behind the seats, 117 in the frunk, an electrically folding rear bench and 2,138 litres loaded flat. Stalkless indicators and touchscreen-only wipers still irritate. Buy it for the packaging and the network, not the interface.

Skoda took the MEB platform, trimmed the fat and priced it properly. From €33,900 the Elroq 50 gives 377 km WLTP from 52 kWh and 145 kW peak charging — 26 minutes to 80%, which is competitive at this money. The €44,180 Elroq 85 is the sweet spot: 77 kWh, 573 km, 175 kW, 6.6 seconds to 100 km/h and a real-world figure in the mid-400s. The chassis is the star. It is supple, quiet and unflustered, with steering that is accurate rather than entertaining, and it only feels its two tonnes on a badly surfaced country road. The 470-litre boot is smaller than an Enyaq's but far better organised, with dividers and cable nets. Interior plastics are honest rather than plush, and the 13-inch screen still buries too much. ADAC ranks it top of its class. On price per usable kilometre in Germany, it is very hard to argue with.

The R5 is the first small EV in years designed around European roads rather than European regulations. From €27,900 the 40 kWh car offers 312 km WLTP; €32,900 buys the 52 kWh version with 416 km, and that is the one to have. Efficiency is the headline — at a steady 90 km/h it sits near 11 kWh/100 km, better than cars costing twice as much. Push to 130 km/h and a 0.32 drag coefficient bites hard: range collapses towards 240 km and wind noise becomes intrusive. Charging is the weak point at 100 kW peak and 31 minutes to 80%, while the 40 kWh car manages only 80 kW. The multi-link rear axle gives it composure and a playful edge that the Citroën and Fiat alternatives simply lack. The 326-litre boot is average and rear headroom is tight. As an urban primary or a second car, it is the most likeable thing on this list.

Six years and several software generations in, the ID.3 has quietly become good. The €36,425 Pro pairs 59 kWh with 434 km WLTP and 165 kW charging — 24 minutes to 80%, quicker than most rivals at the price. The €44,025 Pro S stretches to 79 kWh, 568 km and 185 kW. What sells it now is refinement: suspension that filters broken tarmac better than anything from Stellantis, wind and road noise low enough to make 250 km stints painless, and rear legroom that embarrasses a Golf. It is not entertaining — the steering is accurate and mute — but it is restful, which matters more on a Tuesday. The 385-litre boot is modest for the footprint and there is no frunk. Post-facelift materials are much improved, though the layered menus and touch climate sliders remain a self-inflicted wound. Next to an Elroq it looks pricey. Judged alone, it is a mature, low-drama hatchback.

The ID.4 is the sensible, faintly anonymous choice, and it has aged better than its launch reviews suggested. The €46,335 Pro carries 77 kWh, 572 km WLTP and 175 kW DC charging for a 28-minute 10-80%. Expect 400-430 km in real German motorway use, with consumption around 19-20 kWh/100 km. Performance is adequate rather than urgent — 6.7 seconds to 100 km/h — and it runs short of shove above 120 km/h. Space is where it earns its keep: 543 litres behind the seats, 1,575 folded, and rear legroom that genuinely rivals a Passat. Ride quality is fluid on 19-inch wheels and busier on 20s, while a 10.2 m turning circle makes it easy in a multi-storey. The software is finally usable; the haptic sliders still are not. Against an Enyaq 85 at similar money it loses on boot volume and gains nothing obvious. Competent, well-built, and thoroughly unexciting.

This is the car the ID range was always meant to produce. The €54,105 Pro claims 621 km WLTP from 77 kWh, and ADAC measured 485 km in real testing at 18.1 kWh/100 km — an extraordinary result for a five-metre liftback. DC charging peaks at 190 kW and averages around 130 kW, adding roughly 275 km in twenty minutes, though AC is capped at 11 kW, which is mean at this price. Comfort is the strongest suit in this entire group: adaptive dampers, a three-metre wheelbase, massage seats and rear legroom that shames an A6. The 532-litre load bay sits behind a hatchback aperture, so it swallows awkward objects a Model 3 cannot. The complaints are ergonomic rather than mechanical — touch-only window switches, buried climate controls, no frunk. Expensive next to a Skoda, but as a long-distance instrument it is among the best-riding EVs sold in Europe.

The Highland update turned a promising car into a properly resolved one. At €37,970 the 60 kWh RWD claims 534 km WLTP, and efficiency remains the class benchmark: 15.9 kWh/100 km across 700 km of mixed testing, and roughly 16 kWh/100 km at a sustained 130 km/h. That second figure is the one that matters, because it converts into real motorway range rather than brochure range. Charging is solid rather than spectacular — 175 kW peak, 24 minutes to 80% — on a 400-volt architecture an 800-volt Hyundai will beat, but Supercharger coverage still removes the planning. The retuned rear axle and thicker glass cured the old car's brittleness and drone, though it stays firmer than an ID.7. 594 litres of total storage sounds generous until you meet the saloon boot aperture. Indicator buttons on the wheel and wiper controls in a menu remain bad ideas. As an efficiency instrument, unmatched at the money.

The iX1 sells on badge, seats and driving position rather than electrical engineering. €47,900 buys the eDrive20: 64.7 kWh, 475 km WLTP, 8.3 seconds to 100 km/h. In practice expect 360-380 km, falling towards 330 in a German winter — a long way short of a Kia EV3 costing €6,000 less. Charging is the genuine weakness at 128 kW peak and 33 minutes to 80%, which is 2022-grade hardware in a 2026 market. What you get in exchange is a tightly damped chassis with real body control, excellent seats, a cabin that feels €10,000 dearer than the ID.4's, and a properly usable 490-litre boot. On adaptive dampers the ride is firm-edged but never crashy; on passive suspension and 20-inch wheels it fidgets. The curved iDrive display looks superb and buries heated seats ten taps deep. The enthusiast's compact EV, and the accountant's least favourite.

Kia's numbers do the talking. €41,390 buys the 78 kWh Long Range with 605 km WLTP, a figure nothing else near this price approaches, and 430-490 km is realistic in mild weather. The Standard Range opens the line around €35,990. The catch is the 400-volt architecture: 135 kW peak and 33 minutes from 10-80% means an Elroq with a smaller pack refills faster, so long trips demand patience and good route planning. Dynamically it is soft and safe — 7.7 seconds to 100 km/h, light steering, noticeable body movement over poor surfaces, but excellent isolation once you settle at 120 km/h. The cabin is the class benchmark for usability: real switchgear, twin 12.3-inch displays that respond instantly, a flat rear floor, and a deep underfloor bin beneath the 460-litre boot. Rationally the strongest value here. It just never quite excites.

The facelifted Enyaq is the family EV to beat on packaging. 585 litres behind the seats and 1,710 with the bench folded beats an ID.4 and a Kia EV6, and rear space makes it a credible three-child car. From €44,400 the Enyaq 60 delivers 437 km WLTP from 59 kWh at 165 kW — a brisk 24 minutes to 80%. The €48,900 Enyaq 85 offers 77 kWh and 586 km but oddly caps DC at 135 kW, so 28 minutes is the reality and the cheaper car charges faster. Ride quality is the other strength: settled, quiet, slightly aloof, with steering weighted for the autobahn rather than an Alpine pass. 6.7 seconds to 100 km/h in the 85 is ample. Materials are durable rather than luxurious and the 13-inch screen still handles too much. Identical hardware to a VW ID.4, more boot, less money. That is a difficult argument to lose.

At €23,300 the ë-C3 is the cheapest route into a genuinely competent European EV, and Citroën spent the budget in the right places. The hydraulic-cushion suspension delivers long-wave comfort no rival under €30,000 gets near, though a 2.54 m wheelbase means sharp speed bumps still set it bouncing. The 44 kWh LFP pack claims 327 km WLTP; 250-270 km is honest. Cold-weather charging is the sore point — the 100 kW rating is theoretical, and independent testing recorded barely 35 kW on a chilled 150 kW post, turning a claimed 31-minute 10-80% into the better part of an hour. 11.5 seconds to 100 km/h means motorway merges need forward planning. The 310-litre boot is decent for the class but there is no adjustable floor and no frunk, and the rear bench does not fold flat. Excellent as an urban and regional car. Ask it to cover 500 km and it will disappoint.

The Spring is a quadricycle wearing a hatchback's clothes, and it is refreshingly honest about it. €18,900 buys 25 kWh, 225 km WLTP and 13.7 seconds to 100 km/h — figures that look absurd until you weigh the car. Under a tonne means real consumption near 13-14 kWh/100 km, so 180 km of urban range is achievable and a home tariff makes running costs almost invisible. DC charging is optional and peaks around 34 kW, so 10-80% takes about 38 minutes; treat any autoroute journey as a planning error. Body control is poor, the seats are flat and unsupportive, and crosswinds move it around. But the 308-litre boot is genuinely useful, the controls are gloriously physical, and Euro NCAP's low score is the one number that should give you pause. For a household covering 40 km a day, nothing matches its cost per kilometre. For anything else, look elsewhere.

The Q6 is where the Volkswagen Group's 800-volt PPE platform finally earns its development budget. The €68,800 performance returns 661 km WLTP from 94.9 kWh, and charging is the best here by a clear margin: 269 kW peak, 10-80% in 23 minutes, with enough thermal headroom to do it twice in a day. Prices open at €63,500, which is a lot of money for a cabin that is more screen than substance — material quality does not match the invoice, and the single curved display swallowed switches that should have survived. On air suspension it rides beautifully, gliding over surfaces that upset a BMW iX1 on 21-inch wheels; on steel springs it is merely good. Real consumption near 21 kWh/100 km yields roughly 550 km. 526 litres is adequate rather than generous for the footprint. Technically the most accomplished car on this list, and the hardest to justify.

The Born is what happens when Volkswagen's MEB platform is handed to people who care about the rear axle. €41,450 buys 231 PS driving the back wheels, 0-100 km/h in 6.7 seconds and a chassis that stays composed on broken German B-roads without ever turning brittle. The 59 kWh pack is the sensible choice: 427 km WLTP, roughly 360 km in real use, and — critically — a 165 kW DC peak that clears 10-80% in 24 minutes, among the quickest 400-volt cars in this class. Interior quality beats the ID.3 it shares bones with, though the infotainment still lags a beat behind your inputs and the capacitive sliders remain a solved problem nobody solved. The 385-litre boot is Golf-sized, no more. Rear legroom is genuinely generous. It is not fast in any modern sense, but it is deft, efficient and unusually well damped for the money.

Volvo squeezed a lot into 4,233 mm — arguably too much. The Single Motor Extended Range asks €44,990 for 65 kWh usable, 476 km WLTP and 0-100 km/h in 5.3 seconds, making it quicker than most hot hatches of a decade ago and the fastest thing here per euro. The damping is genuinely well judged; it isolates urban scars far better than the price suggests. Then you sit inside. Every function — mirrors, demist, even your speed — lives in one 12.3-inch portrait screen, and the cost in attention is real, not theoretical. The rear bench is tight for adults and the 318-litre boot is the smallest here bar the Inster. Charging is competent rather than remarkable: 153 kW peak, 10-80% in 28 minutes. Buy it for the drivetrain, the material honesty and the exterior restraint. Don't buy it if you routinely carry people or luggage behind you.

€60,600 is a lot, and BMW knows it. What it buys is the most complete electric saloon under €70,000: 81.3 kWh usable, 505-613 km WLTP depending on wheel choice, and a 205 kW DC peak that reduces 10-80% to a 28-minute coffee. The eDrive40's 340 PS and 5.6 seconds to 100 km/h understate how effortlessly it covers ground — this is a car that sits at 160 km/h on an unrestricted A-road and simply gets on with it, with highway consumption near 20 kWh/100 km keeping 400 km between stops realistic. The ride is taut rather than plush, but body control at speed is a class above the soft-riding German crossovers on this list. The liftback tailgate makes 470 litres far more usable than the figure implies. Rear headroom suffers for the roofline, and the options list is predatory — budget €70,000 as configured. Still the benchmark.

Renault's Scénic revival is the least glamorous car here and quite possibly the smartest buy. €40,400 gets the EV60: 60 kWh, 430 km WLTP, 545 litres of boot and Google-native infotainment that works better than anything Stuttgart or Ingolstadt has shipped. The 170 PS front motor needs 8.6 seconds to 100 km/h and feels every one of its 1,847 kg — this is transport, not entertainment. Charging is the weak link: 130 kW peak and 33 minutes for 10-80%, and the car is arguably at its best on 22 kW AC, where the bidirectional hardware genuinely earns its keep. The ride is competent rather than French-luxurious, and 20-inch wheels introduce a thump the smaller rims avoid. Forward visibility is poor. But the packaging is exceptional for 4.47 metres, the rear seats are adult-grade, and the 87 kWh Long Range version's 625 km makes it one of Europe's real long-distance bargains.

The EQA is a GLA with the combustion parts removed, and it has never stopped feeling like one. €52,205 buys 70.5 kWh usable, 532 km WLTP and a front motor good for 190 PS and 8.6 seconds to 100 km/h — figures that were merely adequate in 2021 and are now conspicuously behind. The real indictment is charging: a 100 kW ceiling and 35 minutes for 10-80%, which on a long autoroute run costs you a genuine half-hour against a Tavascan or Q4 e-tron. The ride is soft and underdamped, floating over crests rather than controlling them, though motorway refinement is excellent and the cabin still feels expensively assembled. Then the boot: 340 litres, less than a Golf, with no proper cable stowage. Quiet, well equipped, reassuringly solid — and roughly €700 more than a better-engineered Audi Q4 45 with 6.5 kWh more usable battery. Badge value only stretches so far.

Peugeot's supermini is the most stylish thing in this price bracket and the most compromised to live with. €37,525 for the 54 kWh car is a serious sum for 4,055 mm of hatchback, though French and German purchase incentives soften it meaningfully. What you get is 433 km WLTP — realistically around 335 km — from 50.8 kWh usable, 156 PS, 8.2 seconds to 100 km/h and a 107 kW DC peak that delivers 10-80% in 28 minutes. That charging figure is genuinely competitive for the segment. The i-Cockpit remains divisive: the tiny wheel and raised binnacle suit some drivers and actively fight others, so sit in one before you sign anything. GT trim's suspension is brittle over poor surfaces; lesser trims ride considerably better. The 309-litre boot is fine for the class, rear legroom is not. Buy it because you want a beautiful small car, not because it's the rational choice.

Toyota's first proper EV launched badly and has been quietly fixed. The 2025 revision brings a 73.1 kWh pack (69 kWh usable), 568 km WLTP, 224 PS and — finally — 150 kW DC charging with battery preconditioning, turning 10-80% into 28 minutes instead of the previous embarrassment. At €47,990 it undercuts the Audi Q4 45 by roughly €5,000 while delivering most of the same competence. The ride is the standout: soft, long-travel and genuinely restful, the closest thing here to a proper touring car. Real-world consumption around 18 kWh/100 km gives a credible 385 km. Against that, the driving position is odd — a high floor and a wheel that never quite lands where you want it — rear legroom suffers from that same floor, and 452 litres is merely average with no frunk to compensate. Not exciting. Very hard to break. For a lot of European households, that's the correct trade.

The Q4 45 is the MEB platform in its most expensively finished form, and since the 2024 update the numbers finally justify the badge: 77 kWh usable, 563 km WLTP, 286 PS to the rear axle, 6.7 seconds to 100 km/h and a 175 kW DC peak that clears 10-80% in 28 minutes. Consumption of about 18.3 kWh/100 km is genuinely good for a car this heavy. Dynamically it is unruffled rather than engaging — the steering tells you nothing, and 21-inch wheels introduce a fidget the standard rims avoid — but the isolation, seat comfort and long-distance manners are exactly what most buyers actually want. 520 litres and a flat, square load bay make it the most practical thing here outside the EQB. At €52,950 it isn't cheap, and Audi still hides the good equipment behind packs. This is nonetheless the VW Group crossover to buy.

Hyundai has done something genuinely difficult: built a 3,825 mm city car that isn't a punishment. €25,400 for the Long Range — well under €22,000 after German incentives — buys 46 kWh usable, 370 km WLTP and around 300 km in realistic mixed use, which is more usable range than city cars costing €10,000 more. The sliding rear seats fold completely flat and the cabin swallows objects a car this size has no business carrying. The compromises are real and unhidden: four seats only, 280 litres of boot, 10.6 seconds to 100 km/h, and an 85 kW ceiling that still means 29 minutes for 10-80% despite the small pack. The ride is soft and forgiving over broken urban surfaces; the steering is inert. It is not entertaining and it is not an autobahn car. As a second car for a European household, nothing at this price comes close.

The EQB's case rests on a single number: seven seats, standard, for €53,514, inside a 4.68-metre body. Nothing else on this list does that. The 250+ gives you 70.5 kWh usable, 506 km WLTP and 495 litres behind the second row, expanding to 1,710 with everything folded. Refinement is the other genuine strength — the motor is inaudible and the boxy shape generates less wind roar than it has any right to. Beyond that, the engineering shows its age. 190 PS and 8.9 seconds to 100 km/h is slow by 2025 standards, the 100 kW DC ceiling means 35 minutes for 10-80%, and the body lollops rather than controls. Deploy the third row and boot space collapses to something a weekly shop would overwhelm. Priced against a Q4 e-tron it looks expensive; priced against any other seven-seat EV under €60,000, it looks like the only option.

The second-generation Kona is a masterclass in packaging and a cautionary tale about pricing. Just 4.36 metres yields 466 litres of boot and rear space that genuinely fits adults behind adults — a Q4-adjacent result from a car two size classes smaller. 65.4 kWh usable returns 514 km WLTP and a realistic 400 km, at roughly 16.8 kWh/100 km, which shames several larger rivals here. Hyundai also kept around thirty physical buttons, which after a week in an EX30 feels like a civil right. The problem is the 400-volt architecture: a 102 kW peak and 41 minutes for 10-80% is poor in 2025, and it makes long European trips slower than the range figure promises. Handling is soft, the steering uncommunicative, and the lane-keeping alerts are hyperactive. At €47,190 it asks Q4 money for a compact crossover. Superb as a high-mileage daily; frustrating the moment you point it at the Alps.

The Tavascan is what the VW ID.5 should have been. Same 77 kWh pack, same MEB underpinnings, but Cupra spent the development budget on damping and drama rather than cost-down. €53,340 buys 542 km WLTP, 286 PS to the rear wheels, 6.8 seconds to 100 km/h and a chassis with genuine rear-drive attitude — it turns in and settles in a way no ID-badged sibling manages. Aerodynamics are the quiet triumph: a 0.26 drag coefficient yields roughly 17.3 kWh/100 km and a credible 445 km in real conditions. Charging peaks at 135 kW for 10-80% in 28 minutes, respectable but no longer class-leading against 800-volt rivals. The 540-litre boot is properly usable, the newest VW Group infotainment is finally quick, and the full-width dashboard spine eats cabin storage. The illuminated badges are a matter of taste. Expensive — but the most interesting car this platform has produced.
